rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable follows the mention of worldly life in v. 23 and stresses its evanescence, alongside related parables in 29:64 and 18:45.
rows.anchor: After the mention of the life of this world in v. 23, v. 24 lays down a parable that draws attention to its evanescent nature

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: The verse addresses people deluded by worldly life who have no concern for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that this verse is aimed at those who are deluded by this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain rejuvenates the earth and produces diverse vegetation; this growth is the earth taking on luster and becoming adorned.
rows.anchor: When rain descends from the sky, the earth is rejuvenated and from it many different types of vegetation spring forth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The colorful herbage and varied benefits of the garden delight its inhabitants.
rows.anchor: With its beautiful herbage and color, the earth’s garden brings delight to its inhabitants because of the multifarious ways in which they can benefit from it

rows.speaker: Kl, N, R, Z
rows.claim: The Command that destroys the garden is understood as a violent wind, torrent, or mighty blast.
rows.anchor: God’s Command, here understood to be a violent wind, torrent, or some kind of mighty blast (Kl, N, R, Z)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: The Command’s arrival by night or day means it can come at any moment.
rows.anchor: by night or by day—that is, at any moment (Th)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Command obliterates the garden’s trees and vegetation, leaving it like a mown field.
rows.anchor: thereby obliterating its trees and vegetation (R), leaving the garden as a mown field

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: One who invests the heart in worldly pleasures suffers immense sorrow and grief when those pleasures leave.
rows.anchor: This verse prompts al-Rāzī to observe, “Such is the one who invests his heart in the pleasures of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers will see worldly life or the interval between death and resurrection as lasting only an hour of the day.
rows.anchor: their life in the world or the interval between their physical death and their resurrection as but an hour of the day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny meeting God suffer loss as a consequence of that denial.
rows.anchor: For the loss the disbelievers will experience as a result of denying their meeting with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In answer to Makkan idolaters demanding hastened punishment, the Prophet has no independent power to bring punishment or benefit; all depends on God’s will.
rows.anchor: neither he nor anyone else possesses the power to bring about God’s Punishment (Q, Th, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each community has a lifespan known only to God and perishes at its end, though it may be punished before its earthly term expires.
rows.anchor: a specific life span known only to God—at the end of which that particular community will perish

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s rhetorical rebuke means that repentance when no alternative remains is too late and will not be accepted.
rows.anchor: “You want to repent now that you have no other alternative? This shall never be accepted from you!” (Kl)

rows.speaker: Aj, Kl
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s body would remain above the sea on raised ground as a sign to later people, unlike the bodies of his hosts.
rows.anchor: Rather, it will be preserved upon a raised surface of earth so that it will be a sign unto those who come after (Aj, Kl)

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, JJ, Kl, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Although “save” is present tense, it refers to earlier messengers and means God saved them.
rows.anchor: “Then we saved Our messengers” (Bg, IK, JJ, Kl, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will deliver Muhammad and his followers from Makkan persecution, as He delivered earlier messengers and their followers from persecutors.
rows.anchor: incumbent upon Us to save the believers means that God will deliver

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd is second among six sūrahs whose openings contain Alif, Lām, Rāʾ and speak of the Book.
rows.anchor: whose opening verses include the letters alif, lām, and rāʾ, and which speak of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah followed Sūrah 10 and belongs to the earlier Makkan period.
rows.anchor: As is clear from its content and message, this sūrah was revealed after Sūrah 10 and thus belongs to the earlier Makkan period (JJ)

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators regard verses 12, 17, and 114 as possible exceptions to the sūrah’s Makkan dating, placing them in Madinah.
rows.anchor: vv. 12, 17, and 114, which are said by many commentators to have been revealed in Madinah (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context of verse 12 places it in the Makkan period, amid the idolaters’ intense opposition to the Prophet’s mission.
rows.anchor: the context of v. 12 clearly situates it in the Makkan period, at the height of the Makkan idolaters’ opposition to the Prophet’s mission

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have said that Hūd and its sister sūrahs turned his hair gray.
rows.anchor: “Hūd and her sisters have turned my hair gray.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah opens by calling Makkan idolaters to worship the one God and warning of punishment if they turn away.
rows.anchor: the Prophet’s call to the Makkan idolaters to worship the one true God (v. 2), promising them punishment if they turn away from this call (v. 3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses the Makkans’ concealed animosity toward the Prophet.
rows.anchor: their concealed animosity toward him (v. 5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses the Makkans’ rejection of the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: their rejection of the Resurrection (v. 7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses their outrageous demand that the Prophet demonstrate his message’s truth.
rows.anchor: their outrageous demands that he demonstrate the veracity of his message (v. 12)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses the Makkans’ accusation that the Quran was fabricated.
rows.anchor: their accusations that the Quran was fabricated (v. 13)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long narrative section recounts Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Abraham, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Moses, with each prophet’s passage specified in the source.
rows.anchor: the stories of the prophets Noah (vv. 25–48), Hūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Hūd in verses 50–60 gives the sūrah its title.
rows.anchor: Hūd (vv. 50–60, from which the sūrah derives its title)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative section has many parallels with 7:59–136.
rows.anchor: This section has many parallels with 7:59–136

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts console the Prophet amid the Makkan idolaters’ growing hostility toward him and the believers.
rows.anchor: serving here to console the Prophet in the environment of the Makkan idolaters’ growing hostility toward him and the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They show that earlier prophets faced great trials in delivering their message and ultimately overcame opponents with God’s help.
rows.anchor: It demonstrates to the Prophet the manner in which the previous prophets also faced great trials in delivering their message to their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stories are related to make the Prophet’s heart firm, one of the main effects of Quranic sacred history.
rows.anchor: these stories have been related to make his heart firm (v. 120)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah encourages the Prophet and believers to persist in the prescribed prayers.
rows.anchor: to persist in the prescribed prayers (v. 114)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah encourages patience.
rows.anchor: be patient (v. 115)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah encourages trust in God.
rows.anchor: trust in God (v. 123)
